title: Why You're 99.9999% Empty Space (And Still Solid)
description:
Every human on Earth could fit inside one sugar cube. Professor Ved shrinks you down to the atom: a stadium-sized atom with a marble for a nucleus, the 1909 gold-foil experiment where 1 in 8,000 alpha particles bounced back, why 'mostly empty' is only half the story (electrons are spread-out clouds), why you don't fall through your chair (electric repulsion + the Pauli exclusion principle), neutron stars, and where your mass really comes from.

Sources: Geiger & Marsden, 'On a Diffuse Reflection of the alpha-Particles' (Proc. Royal Society, 1909); Rutherford (Phil. Mag., 1911) and his 1936 Cambridge lecture; Dyson & Lenard, 'Stability of Matter' (J. Math. Phys., 1967); NASA via Space.com on neutron stars; Jefferson Lab on atoms in the body; Ethan Siegel (Big Think), 'You are not mostly empty space'.

scenes.say: This sugar cube could hold every human on Earth. All *eight billion* of us.
Sounds impossible. But stick with me, and you'll see why it's true, why you've never really touched anything, and why you still don't fall through your chair.
Because almost everything around you, the table, the cup, the people... you. It's mostly empty space. So let's find out how empty.
Everything is made of atoms, and atoms are tiny. Line up *ten million* of them, and you'd cover just one millimetre.
Your body holds about seven billion billion billion atoms. That's a seven with twenty-seven zeros.
Too small to picture. So let's cheat. Let's blow one single atom up to the size of a *football stadium*.
Walk down to the centre spot... and there's the nucleus. About the size of a *marble*.
It's about a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself. And that marble holds more than *99.9 percent* of the atom's mass.
The electrons? They're way out in the back rows of the stands. And between the marble and the seats...
...there's no air. No stuff. Just a whole stadium of *nothing*.
But how do we actually know this? In 1909, in Manchester, the physicist Ernest Rutherford gave two of his team a strange job.

layers.title: Manchester, England
layers.sub: 1909. The physics laboratory of Ernest Rutherford

scenes.say: Hans Geiger and a twenty-year-old student, Ernest Marsden, fired tiny *alpha particles* at a sheet of gold, beaten thinner than paper.
Each particle that hit a screen made a tiny flash of light. So they sat in the dark, counting flashes through a microscope. One. By. One.
At the time, scientists pictured the atom as a soft pudding of charge. So the particles should sail straight through.

layers.title: J. J. THOMSON, 1904
layers.text: The atom: a sphere of positive charge, with electrons dotted through it like plums in a pudding.

scenes.say: And almost all of them did.
But about one in every *eight thousand*... bounced right back.
Rutherford later said it was as incredible as firing a fifteen-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper... and having it come back and hit you.

layers.text: “It was quite the most incredible event that has ever happened to me in my life. It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.”

scenes.say: The only explanation: nearly all the atom's mass is packed into one tiny, dense core.

layers.title: The Scattering of Alpha and Beta Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom

scenes.say: In 1911, Rutherford published the idea. We call that core the *nucleus*.
Now, a fair warning. 'Mostly empty space' is the classic picture. But many physicists say it's a little misleading.
Electrons aren't little balls zooming round the stands. Quantum physics says each one is *spread out*, like a fog, filling the whole atom.

layers.text: SEE: E. SIEGEL, 'YOU ARE NOT MOSTLY EMPTY SPACE'

scenes.say: So which is it? If you ask where the mass sits, the atom is almost all empty. If you ask where the electron can be, it fills the space. Both are true. They just answer different questions.

layers.title: Q: WHERE IS THE MASS?
layers.text: Almost all of it in the nucleus. By mass, the atom is nearly empty.

layers.title: Q: WHERE CAN THE ELECTRON BE?
layers.text: Everywhere in the atom. By where the electron can be, it is full.

layers.title: Why you don't fall through your chair

scenes.say: So if atoms are that roomy... why don't you sink straight through your chair?
Two reasons. First: the outside of every atom is electrons, and electrons all carry a *negative* charge. Like charges push each other away. Hard.
Second: a quantum rule called the *Pauli exclusion principle*. No two electrons can squeeze into the same state. So atoms refuse to collapse into each other.

layers.title: Wolfgang Pauli
layers.sub: physicist, proposed the exclusion principle in 1925

scenes.say: In 1967, the physicists Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved that without this rule, ordinary matter would *collapse*. Putting two objects together would release energy like an atomic bomb.

layers.text: No Pauli rule = matter collapses. Two objects meeting = an atomic bomb.

scenes.say: So when you shake someone's hand, your atoms never bump like two billiard balls. What you feel as touch... is electrons pushing back.
Some physicists say that push is simply what touching means. Fair enough. Either way, it's a force you feel, not a wall of stuff.

layers.text:
Me: touching grass.
The grass: technically, no.

scenes.say: Now, back to our sugar cube. Take every atom in every person on Earth, and squeeze out all that empty space.
All eight billion of us would fit in a cube about this size. But it would still weigh as much as all of us. *Hundreds of millions* of tonnes.
Which is bad news for the table.
And the universe actually does this. When a giant star dies, its core can collapse into a *neutron star*.
Gravity squeezes so hard that electrons are pushed into protons, turning them into neutrons, packed shoulder to shoulder. Almost no empty space left.
A neutron star packs more mass than our Sun into a ball about *twenty kilometres* across. Roughly the size of a city.
A sugar cube of neutron star would weigh about a *billion tonnes*. As much as the whole human race.

layers.title: So what are you made of?

scenes.say: One last twist. Even the marble isn't really solid stuff. It's made of protons and neutrons, and they're made of *quarks*.
And the quarks' own mass is only about one percent of it. The other ninety-nine percent is *energy*: the strong force, holding them together. E equals m c squared, at work inside you.
So you're not made of tiny hard balls. You're made of *forces*: electric pushes, quantum rules, and trapped energy.
Solid isn't stuff. It's a *push* you can feel.
If that blew your mind a little, subscribe. Every week, one big idea, made simple.
